parakeet: Confession becomes risky. Accountability is replaced by concealment because exposure carries collective consequences. Moral growth stalls not because people don't care, but because the cost of openness is way too high. Over time, this conditions people to police themselves and each other. Anxiety replaces trust as the glue holding the community together. The safest behavior is not ethical reflection, but invisibility. People learn how to avoid being noticed rather than how to repair harm. Collective guilt creates self-policing communities. Formal enforcement becomes almost unnecessary because surveillance is internalized. Neighbors monitor neighbors, families monitor members. Social pressure enforces conformity more efficiently than external punishment ever could. Informal reporting, exclusion, and shaming becomes tools of moral regulation, all justified as protecting the group. This system is remarkably durable. When everyone is responsible for everyone else's purity, authority does not need to watch constantly. The community does it for them. Fear becomes a stabilizing force. Order is maintained not through justice, but through mutual vulnerability to punishment. Leviticus reveals the cost of this logic clearly. One person's mistake becomes everyone's threat. On the surface, Leviticus is often dismissed as an ancient relic, an odd collection of rules from a distant world that no longer applies. And historically, that's partly true.
